conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you feel emotionally supported now that your baby has arrived. To do that, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (EPDS). It’s simply 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it’s not a test of your parenting—just a way to check on your emotional well-being. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and if any question feels hard, we’ll pause and talk it through. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.

In the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]  
I… I can laugh sometimes—like when my husband made a silly joke yesterday—but mostly it feels kind of forced. It’s like the humor’s there, but it’s muffled, you know? I almost feel guilty laughing when I’m this tired.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah... I guess I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. It feels kind of distant, like I’m watching myself laugh instead of really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs softly, eyes on the blanket]  
Not really. I mean, I used to get excited about little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee—but lately even the thought of getting us both dressed and out the door feels exhausting. I’m not dreading everything, I just… don’t look forward to much anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quietly] Yeah... sometimes. Like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I start thinking it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not holding him the “best” way or I missed some cue. I know logically babies just cry, but in the moment my head jumps to “I messed up.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the edge of the blanket around my fingers]  
Mostly at night, when the house is quiet. My heart will race and I’ll run through all these “what-ifs”—what if his breathing sounds weird, what if the rash on his neck is something serious, what if I fall asleep too hard and don’t hear him. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes I’ll be rocking the baby in the chair and suddenly feel like I can’t catch my breath—like the walls are inching in. It’s not a full panic, but my chest gets tight and I have to stand up, walk to the window, remind myself we’re safe. It passes in a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get him down for a nap, and the dishes are still stacked, bottles need sterilizing, the dog’s whining to go out—then he wakes up early and I feel like I failed at the one quiet moment I had. I keep thinking, “I just need to push through,” but it piles up fast.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[glances down, voice softer]  
It’s not so much that I’m lying there sobbing… but when I finally crawl into bed, my mind just keeps spinning—did I count the wet diapers right, did I fasten the swaddle tight enough, when will he wake next. I end up staring at the ceiling or checking the baby cam every half hour. I probably get four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time… not every minute, but it kind of drifts in. Like when I’m feeding him at 3 a.m. and the house is dark, I’ll suddenly feel weepy for no clear reason. It’s not a constant cloud, but it keeps popping up and I can’t always shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really… I mean, I’ve teared up a couple of times—once when I couldn’t get him to latch and my milk was spraying everywhere—but actual crying? Maybe once this week, and it was short. Mostly I just feel tired and flat, not weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]

No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom he deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, intermittent tearfulness, diminished pleasure/interest (anhedonia)
- Daily anxiety, nocturnal worry, episodic chest tightness/“walls closing in”
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care
- Feeling overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty completing tasks
- Initial insomnia and middle insomnia linked to rumination about infant safety
- Fatigue, flat affect; laughter described as “distant”
- Denies suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts, or intent

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, worse at night, duration ≥ 2 weeks, causing subjective distress and functional impairment.

Screening significance:  
Positive indicators for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid anxiety symptoms; no current safety concerns.

Recommended next step: Formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and evaluation for treatment/support options.
